title: Australia’s FMCG workforce challenge is becoming structural
gist: Oxford Economics Australia modelling for the Australian Food and Grocery Council finds demand will exceed workforce supply by 2035 in all five critical food-and-grocery manufacturing occupations studied — packers, food and drink factory workers, forklift drivers, purchasing and supply logistics clerks, and manufacturing production managers. The operative finding is that the cause differs by occupation: retention for packers, age-driven attrition (about 60% of forklift drivers leaving by 2035) for others, and demand outrunning supply for production managers, so a generic 'more workers' response misallocates capital.

themes.theme: 2035 supply-demand gap in Australian food manufacturing

insights.claim: Australia's food and grocery manufacturing sector employs nearly 300,000 people and sits inside an historically tight labour market, with shortages concentrated in operational, technical and trade-related roles.
insights.speaker: Adric Kam
insights.so_what: Sizes the labour exposure behind Australian packaged-food supply chains: a ~300k headcount base whose operational roles are already scarce means unit labour cost and throughput risk are live inputs to FMCG margin forecasts.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics Australia modelling for the Australian Food and Grocery Council projects that demand will exceed workforce supply in all five studied occupations — packers, food and drink factory workers, forklift drivers, purchasing and supply logistics clerks, and manufacturing production managers — by 2035.
insights.speaker: Adric Kam
insights.so_what: A decade-long, five-for-five shortfall is a structural cost floor rather than a cyclical squeeze — watch it as persistent wage pressure and a capex trigger for automation in Australian food processing.

insights.claim: The framing of Australian food-manufacturing labour shortage as 'becoming structural' rests on causes embedded in age profiles and occupational mobility rather than on a temporary demand spike, implying the gap does not self-correct with the cycle.
insights.speaker: Adric Kam
insights.so_what: Structural means unmodelled by cyclical labour forecasts — position for durable wage/throughput pressure in Australian food processing rather than mean reversion.

themes.theme: Diagnose-the-cause framework beats headline shortage number

insights.claim: The most decision-relevant result of the five-occupation workforce study is not the aggregate shortfall but that the underlying cause of workforce pressure differs substantially between occupations.
insights.speaker: Adric Kam
insights.so_what: Gives a screening lens for any labour-constrained sector: ask which mechanism (ageing, retention, entry pathway, demand growth) binds before pricing the fix or the policy response.
insights.quote: the most important finding is not the aggregate number. It is that the underlying cause of workforce pressure differs substantially between occupations

insights.claim: Treating a multi-occupation labour gap as a single general shortage of workers risks investing in solutions that do not address the actual binding constraint.
insights.speaker: Adric Kam
insights.so_what: A direct warning that headline 'skills shortage' spending — training subsidies, migration quotas — can be wasted capital; scrutinise workforce policy announcements for occupation-level diagnosis before assuming efficacy.
insights.quote: Treating the challenge simply as a general shortage of workers risks investing in solutions that do not address the underlying constraint.
insights.locator: Australia’s FMCG workforce pressures are significant

insights.claim: Australian FMCG workforce pressures are characterised as significant but manageable, conditional on industry and government responding to the particular cause affecting each occupation rather than to the aggregate.
insights.speaker: Adric Kam
insights.so_what: The base case is not collapse but dispersion — outcomes split between firms and jurisdictions that diagnose correctly and those that do not, creating relative-performance spread inside the same sector.
insights.locator: Australia’s FMCG workforce pressures are significant

themes.theme: Packers: a retention leak, not an intake problem

insights.claim: For packers in Australian food and grocery manufacturing, education and migration deliver significant inflows of new workers, but those inflows are more than offset by workers moving into other occupations and industries, making retention rather than intake the central constraint.
insights.speaker: Adric Kam
insights.so_what: Where outflow exceeds inflow, migration and training expansion produce leakage not headcount — a useful test for whether an economy's immigration lever actually reaches the roles it targets.
insights.locator: For packers, retention is the central challenge

insights.claim: Because packer shortages stem from occupational churn, increasing training places alone is insufficient and employers must address job quality, shift design, supervision, working conditions and career progression.
insights.speaker: Adric Kam
insights.so_what: Implies a real cost line item — better shift design and supervision are opex, not a subsidised program — so margin models for low-skill-intensive food processing should carry a rising labour-quality cost.
insights.quote: Increasing training places alone will therefore be insufficient
insights.locator: For packers, retention is the central challenge

themes.theme: Age-profile cliff in forklift and factory floor roles

insights.claim: Around 60% of Australia's current forklift driver workforce is expected to leave through retirement and other natural attrition by 2035.
insights.speaker: Adric Kam
insights.so_what: A near-two-thirds turnover of a core materials-handling occupation over a decade is a hard, demography-locked deadline — it strengthens the investment case for warehouse automation and autonomous materials handling in Australian logistics.
insights.quote: Around 60% of the current workforce is expected to leave through retirement and other natural attrition by 2035.
insights.locator: Forklift drivers face a different problem

insights.claim: More than 40% of today's food and drink factory workers in Australia are expected to leave the workforce by 2035 due to an ageing age profile.
insights.speaker: Adric Kam
insights.so_what: Two of the sector's largest occupations lose 40-60% of incumbents within the decade — quantifies the replacement-hiring burden that will compete for the same shrinking labour pool.
insights.quote: more than 40% of today’s workers expected to leave over the same period
insights.locator: Forklift drivers face a different problem

insights.claim: Because forklift-driver and factory-worker attrition is largely embedded in the existing age profile, the effective levers are early recruitment, succession planning, knowledge transfer and retention of experienced workers rather than demand-side management.
insights.speaker: Adric Kam
insights.so_what: Age-embedded outflows are already determined and cannot be reversed by policy — the only variable is lead time, so firms starting succession pipelines now hold a measurable operational advantage.

themes.theme: Technology raises rather than reduces skilled labour demand

insights.claim: Workforce supply for manufacturing production managers in Australian food and grocery is expected to grow, but not quickly enough to meet rising demand, while purchasing and supply logistics clerks face both growing demand and workforce outflows.
insights.speaker: Adric Kam
insights.so_what: Growing-but-lagging supply in supervisory and supply-chain roles is where wage escalation concentrates — a leading indicator for white-collar operational salary inflation inside manufacturing.

insights.claim: Technological change in food and grocery manufacturing does not simply reduce labour requirements; it increases demand for people capable of managing production systems, coordinating complex supply chains and integrating new technologies into operations.
insights.speaker: Adric Kam
insights.so_what: Cuts against the straightforward automation-displaces-labour narrative: automation capex in manufacturing creates a complementary hiring requirement, so payback models that assume pure headcount savings understate cost.

themes.theme: Workforce capacity planned like production capacity

insights.claim: The recommended common priority for food and grocery manufacturers is to plan workforce capacity as deliberately as production capacity — identifying which occupations could constrain growth and diagnosing whether pressure arises from ageing, retention, entry pathways or demand.
insights.speaker: Adric Kam
insights.so_what: Elevates labour from an HR line to a capacity-planning constraint alongside plant and equipment — a diligence question to put to any labour-intensive manufacturer.
insights.quote: plan workforce capacity as deliberately as production capacity
insights.locator: Individual businesses will experience these pressures differently

insights.claim: Failure to intervene early on occupation-specific labour constraints translates into lost production, increased operational risk and delayed investment for food and grocery manufacturers.
insights.speaker: Adric Kam
insights.so_what: Names the transmission channel from labour shortage to financial outcome — delayed capex and lost volume — which is where the shortage shows up in earnings rather than in wage lines alone.
insights.quote: before shortages translate into lost production, increased operational risk or delayed investment
insights.locator: Individual businesses will experience these pressures differently

insights.claim: Exposure to these workforce pressures is firm-specific, varying with a business's workforce composition, production processes and location, so sector-level shortage statistics understate the dispersion between individual manufacturers.
insights.speaker: Adric Kam
insights.so_what: Argues against trading the theme at index level — the differentiation is at the single-name and single-site level, favouring bottom-up screening of workforce age profiles and location.
insights.quote: Individual businesses will experience these pressures differently depending on their workforce, production processes and location.
